## Overview

The Paiwan (Paiwan: *Kacalisian*; Chinese: 排灣; pinyin: Páiwān) are an Indigenous people of Taiwan who speak Paiwan, a Formosan language of the Austronesian language family. In 2014, Paiwan people numbered 96,334, approximately 17.8% of Taiwan’s total Indigenous population, making them the second-largest Indigenous group. Most live in the southern chain of the Central Mountain Range, from Damumu Mountain and the upper Wuluo River in the north to the Hengchun Peninsula in the south, as well as in the hills and coastal plains of southeastern Taiwan. Paiwan society has hereditary classes and an aristocracy. Its folk culture includes distinctive ceremonies, tattoo traditions, embroidered clothing, wooden carving, shamanism, and the double-pipe nose flute known as *lalingedan*.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Embroidered clothing** — Embroidery is commonly made in bright colors on dark, often black, backgrounds. It is used to tell stories, preserve memories, and communicate legends and folktales. Clothing patterns and elaborate designs distinguish social class, gender, ceremonial use, and personal achievement.

**Noble clothing** — Intricate and grand patterns, totems, and clothing are reserved for nobles and the chief. Designs containing human heads, human figures, or hundred pace vipers distinguish people of high class from other members of Paiwan society.

**Ceremonial dress** — In solemn ceremonies, men wear ceremonial headwear, long vests, leg coverings, and sword baldrics. Dance attire does not differ from ordinary clothing, although people commonly wear their finest clothes for special occasions.

**Motif vocabulary.** Human heads and ancestral spirits, protection; human figures and hundred pace vipers, high status and power; the Sun and Sun god, nobility; warriors and crossed-shaped patterns, shamanic protection; flowers and grass, ordinary people; hunting knives and animals, common designs; butterflies, innocent young girls.

### Clothing & dress

Paiwan clothing distinguishes societal class, gender, and ceremonies. Earlier materials included bark fibers and pelts; linen, cotton, and wool fabrics later became popular. Men wear circular-collar, long-sleeved, short chest coverings with buttons down the front, together with kilts and a shawl worn over one shoulder. Women wear circular-collar robes buttoned along the right side, with panel skirts and leggings. They also wear head scarves, elaborate head rings, or forehead bands. In solemn ceremonies, men add ceremonial headwear, long vests, leg coverings, and sword baldrics. Mothers personally made traditional clothing for their children when they grew up and approached marriage. Noble and chiefly clothing is marked by elaborate patterns, totems, and motifs unavailable to ordinary people.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Paiwan wooden carvings include images of human heads, snakes, deer, and geometric designs. The sources also describe the construction of the *lalingedan*, or double-pipe nose flute, from two nodes of bamboo: one pipe has finger holes and the other does not. A heated iron rod pierces the holes and makes the air hole, while geometric designs are carved onto the finished instrument.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Tattooed hands are a tradition of both Paiwan and Rukai peoples. Noble women traditionally received hand tattoos as a rite of passage into adulthood. Shamans tattooed different patterns according to personal background, while less noble women could receive tattoos only after paying a substantial price and gaining community approval. Their designs differed from those of noblewomen. The painful process represented dignity, honor, and the suffering a person could endure, and was governed by taboos. Pregnant women could not watch the process, and spectators were not allowed to sneeze. In February 2015, Li Lin, described as the oldest Paiwan person with hand tattoos, died at the age of 102; she began receiving her tattoos at 14.

## Music & performance

The *lalingedan*, or double-pipe nose flute, is a symbol of Paiwan musical heritage. It consists of a melody pipe, the *qivuivu*, and a drone pipe, the *zemangrau*. The pipe with finger holes produces the principal melody, while the other emits a steady droning sound. Traditionally, only noblemen or accomplished hunters could perform on the instrument, and in Traditional Paiwan Society it was associated with social status.

The nose flute was used in courtship, funerals, harvest festivals, weddings, and other ceremonial contexts. Its sound is associated with love, longing, sorrow, and mourning. The instrument’s construction includes five finger holes, an air hole made with a heated iron rod, and carved geometric designs resembling the markings of the Hundred Pacer Snake. The sources describe its sound as a breathy timbre produced by nasal exhalation and connect it with the “voice of the soul” and the calls of the Hundred-pace Snake.

Modern adaptations introduced six-hole designs and twelve-tone equal temperament. In 2011, the Paiwan nose flute was officially designated as a National Important Traditional Art. Pairang Pavavalung (Hsu Kun-chung) and Gilegilau Paqalius (Xie Shui-neng) were recognized as “Living National Treasures” for technical mastery and cultural transmission. The sources also name Sauniaw Tjuveljevelj’s “NASI” (2007), “Brothers Who Sing of Love and Longing” (2011), and “Minasi” (2017).

## Festivals & rituals

Paiwan ceremonies include **Masalut** and **Maljeveq**. Masalut celebrates the rice harvest, while Maljeveq commemorates ancestors or gods. In Taiwan, the Bataul branch holds a major sacrifice called *maleveq* every five years, inviting ancestral spirits to come and bless the community.

*Djemuljat* is an activity within Maleveq in which participants thrust bamboo poles into cane balls symbolizing human heads. The sources also connect the nose flute with funerals, harvest festivals, weddings, courtship, and other ceremonies. Paiwan society has a “five-yearly rite” connected with marriage: marriage-seeking men attempt to cut down as many trees as possible and offer the firewood to the family of the girl they wish to marry.

## Foodways

The sources mention rice harvests in connection with the Masalut ceremony.

## Oral tradition & literature

A Paiwan origin myth states that ancestors lived on Dawu mountain, also called Tawushan, in a place called “Paiwan,” where heaven is said to exist. Because Paiwan people spread from that location, the place name was adopted as the group name. According to some group members, “Paiwan” also means “human being.” Embroidery is used to tell stories and share memories and legends or folktales. The sources identify *The Younger Sister Marries the Snake* in the “See also” section. They also name Ahronglong Sakinu as a Paiwan writer.

## Language & religion

Paiwan, also called *Vinuculjan* ([vinutsuʎan]), is a native language of southern Taiwan. It is spoken as a first language by the Paiwan and is a Formosan language of the Austronesian family. It is also one of Taiwan’s national languages. The sources describe dialect zones including southern and central, central, northernmost, northwestern, east-central, and eastern areas, with named varieties such as Kuɬaɬau, Tjuaqatsiɬay, Ɬarəkrək, Tjukuvuɬ, Kaviangan, Tjaɬakavus, Makazayazaya, Tjariḍik, Tjavuaɬi, and Tjakuvukuvuɬ.

Traditionally, Paiwan people were polytheists. Shamanism was inherited by bloodline and was an important part of Paiwan culture, although a decline in the number of shamans led to concern that rituals could be lost and contributed to the founding of a shamanism school. Thousands converted to Christianity in the late 1940s and 1950s. The Presbyterian church in Taiwan reports 14,900 Paiwan members meeting in 96 congregations, and the New Testament has been translated into Paiwan. The Catholic Church is also active.
